lines.head: Introduction
sentences: Anaphylaxis.
What every Ambulance Officer needs to know.

lines.head: What it is
sentences: Anaphylaxis is a severe allergic reaction, and it can be life threatening.
Treat it as a medical emergency that needs treatment straight away.
It can follow a mild or moderate reaction, so keep watching.

lines.head: The signs
sentences: Look for difficult or noisy breathing.
Swelling of the tongue, or a tight throat.
A hoarse voice, or trouble talking.
A wheeze, or a persistent cough.
Persistent dizziness, or collapse.
And young children may be pale and floppy.

lines.head: When to give adrenaline
sentences: Suspect anaphylaxis? Then look for three things.
Low blood pressure.
Severe bronchospasm.
Or severe breathing distress, from swelling in the airway.
Any one of those is enough. Give adrenaline.

lines.head: Basic care
sentences: Lay the patient flat, unless their breathing is difficult.
Don't let them stand, and don't let them walk.
Remove the trigger if you can.
And request clinical support.

lines.head: The auto-injector
sentences: If the patient has an anaphylaxis plan on hand, follow it.
And if they carry their own auto-injector, use it first.

lines.head: Using an EpiPen
sentences: Take the blue cap off.
Push the orange end firmly against the middle of the thigh, until it clicks.
Then hold it there for ten seconds or more.
You can go through clothing if you need to.
Then gently massage the spot for ten seconds.

lines.head: No auto-injector
sentences: No auto-injector? Call the EOC Clinician.
They may advise intramuscular adrenaline.
That's 10 micrograms per kilogram, up to a single maximum of 500 micrograms.
And further doses, if they're needed.

lines.head: The dose
sentences: So, a 20 kilogram child may be advised 200 micrograms.
And from 50 kilograms up, the dose is capped at 500 micrograms.

lines.head: Asthma and transport
sentences: Someone with known asthma and an allergy has sudden trouble breathing?
Treat it as anaphylaxis first, before any asthma medication.
Continue basic care, transport promptly, and let the receiving facility know you're coming.
Every allergy patient goes to a health facility, even if they seem to recover.

lines.head: Wrap-up
sentences: So. Look for the signs.
Lay them flat.
Give adrenaline early.
Use the auto-injector first.
And always transport.
Now, have a go with the adrenaline checker on this page.
